cards.title: Local Wikipedia: Wikipedia, but only for things a half hour walk from you

depth.text: someone made a **Local Wikipedia** for things within a **half-hour walk** of you

It uses **geocoded Wikipedia pages**. If there are fewer than **25 things** close to you, it takes the closest 25 within about 6 miles; when there are more than 500 things, it includes only the closest **500**. Your location stays in the browser, and shared links don't include it.

depth.text: Dijkstra argued that programming computers in our **native tongues** would make life **harder, not easier**
**Formal symbols** help rule out nonsense, Dijkstra says. He argues that switching to native-language instructions could **add work on both sides**, not simply make programming easier.

cards.title: Docker is weird

depth.text: someone built their own container runtime and found Docker is **five Linux features in a trenchcoat**

The post explains that containers use **namespaces**, **cgroups** and networking features, while Docker turns **image folders** into a process's new root directory. It also says runc runs a C module before Go’s runtime initializes so it can make some system calls.

cards.camps: Two camps: the article says Docker’s daemon usually runs as root; a commenter says Docker does not need root.

comments.text: Hi, I'm the creator of Docker and came across this post. It's always fun to see other engineers think about how you designed a system. I haven't been involved in developing Docker in many years, but it's a fun trip down memory lane. I'm happy to answer any questions you may have.

What made Docker unique IMO is not the container technology itself. I used chroot 20 years ago and it worked just fine. Yes, no network namespaces; no process namespaces, but I don't even think these are that important. What made Docker unique were there things: 1. Dockerfile concept. Building images layer by layer. Caching layers. Everything in a single file. It made possible to iterate on image…

I prefer Podman most of the time, but Docker is/was amazing and a great DX put on top of the so called "5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat". That's the selling point, it's super lightweight and takes full advantage of the OS features that were already there (or being developed) but were awkward to use and required tons of specialized knowledge.

Always nice to see someone demystifying a complex thing by learning the building blocks it's made from. Knowing this, you might find rootless Podman's fork-exec method of starting containers to be more sensible. I certainly do. No root, no daemon, no socket. If you want to learn more about the Linux Kernel namespaces which work together to make a container, this LWN series is really good…

cards.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale

depth.text: someone used **AI** to prove that some software **won't crash** under specific conditions

Anthropic and Theorem had Claude prove no crashes for **239 entry points** across **123 OSS-Fuzz libraries**, on inputs up to **64 MB** under the modeled setup. The proofs cover compiled RISC-V binaries, but the authors stress that this doesn't mean the libraries are bug-free.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see LLM-written proofs as a practical way to catch bugs and make verification more common; others say proving code against a spec doesn't show the spec matches reality, or worry agents will hit a scaling wall.

cards.title: Hedra is a 3D open world game I wrote from scratch while in highschool

depth.text: someone's **high-school project** became Hedra, a **3D game and engine** with about **100k lines of code**

The creator started it at **around age 15** to learn OpenGL. The RPG has **four classes**, each with two specializations, plus **procedurally generated worlds and quests**. Only player contents and the world seed are saved; the rest is created at runtime.

cards.camps: Two camps: some find the high-school game built without AI humbling; others question what 'wrote from scratch' means, including whether autocomplete counts.

glossary.geocoded pages: Pages linked to a place on a map, so a nearby search can find them.
glossary.wrapper: A small tool that gives an existing tool a different, often easier, way for people to use it.
glossary.natural language programming: Giving a computer instructions in everyday speech instead of a programming language.
glossary.formal symbolism: A set of written symbols with fixed rules, so instructions have a precise meaning.
glossary.interface: The names and details other code can use from a crate, without needing its inner workings.
glossary.compiler: A tool that turns code you write into a program a computer can run.
glossary.specification: A written description of what a program should do.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.frontier models: The most capable AI models a company is developing.
glossary.commodification: When a product becomes widely available and harder to distinguish from similar products, making it tougher to charge more.
glossary.application-side: The products people build with a technology, rather than the underlying technology itself.
glossary.utility side: Selling the basic service or tool that other people use to build products.
glossary.acquihiring: Buying a company mainly to bring its employees onto your team.
glossary.Jevons Paradox: The idea that when something gets more efficient, people may use more of it overall.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.moat: An advantage that makes it hard for competitors to take customers away from a business.
glossary.runway: How long a business can keep paying its bills with the money it has.
glossary.VC: Venture capitalists: investors who put money into companies hoping they will grow and earn a return.
glossary.bootstrapped: A business started using its founders’ money or its own earnings, rather than outside investment.
glossary.hustle culture: The idea that success requires working extremely hard, often at the cost of life outside work.
glossary.unicorn: A startup valued at a billion dollars or more.
glossary.tech debt: Extra cleanup work left behind when software choices make future changes harder.
glossary.lifestyle business: A business built to support a comfortable life for its owners, rather than to grow as fast as possible.
glossary.MIVD: Netherlands Defense Intelligence and Security Service: the Dutch government agency described as monitoring Kushner’s phone.
glossary.GRU: General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation: the Russian organization the article says the operative had belonged to.
glossary.signatory: Someone authorized to access an account and potentially make transactions, even if they do not own it.
glossary.slush fund: A shared pool of money kept off the books for political or diplomatic goals.
glossary.training data: The examples and text used to teach an AI system how to respond.
glossary.system prompt: Extra instructions set before a conversation that guide how the AI answers.
glossary.container runtime: A program that sets up a container and starts the process inside it.
glossary.namespaces: A Linux feature that gives a process its own view of things like other processes or the network.
glossary.cgroups: A Linux feature that lets the system manage a set of running programs together.
glossary.chroot: A command that makes a folder act like the top of a process’s file system.
glossary.syscall: A request a program sends to the operating system to do something on its behalf.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.daemon: A program that runs in the background and handles a task without being started each time.
glossary.rootless: Running without needing the highest level of permission on the computer.
glossary.a la carte: Choosing and paying for individual items instead of getting a fixed bundle.
glossary.cloud streaming: Playing a game running on a remote computer while your device receives the picture and sends your controls back.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.thin client: A simple device that mostly shows what another, more powerful computer is doing.
glossary.input latency: The delay between pressing a button and seeing the game react.
glossary.free-to-play: A game you can start playing without paying for the game itself.
glossary.walled garden: A service that keeps you within one company's products and limits what else you can use.
glossary.reverse engineering: Figuring out how a program works by examining the program itself.
glossary.formal verification: Checking a claim using precise rules, often with a computer.
glossary.fuzzing: Testing software with lots of varied inputs to see whether it breaks.
glossary.entry point: A front door into a program where tests can feed it inputs.
glossary.RISC-V: A processor design that sets out the basic instructions software runs on.
glossary.Rocq: A tool that checks whether a proof meets the claim it is meant to establish.
glossary.spec: A written description of what a software feature should do.
glossary.1FA: One-factor authentication: a login that checks one kind of proof, such as a password or code.
glossary.OTP: One-time password: a code meant to work for one login or for a short time.
glossary.brute-force: Repeatedly trying possible codes until one works.
glossary.rate-limit: Set a cap on how many times someone can try something in a period of time.
glossary.endpoint: A specific web address where a service can receive a request.
glossary.search space: All the possible codes someone could try.
glossary.CA: Certificate Authority: an organization that checks requests and issues certificates.
glossary.OpenGL: A set of commands apps use to draw graphics.
glossary.low-poly: A visual style that uses simple shapes and few flat surfaces, often giving objects a blocky look.
glossary.procedural generation: A way for a game to make its world or quests automatically from rules, instead of having someone design every part.
glossary.voxel: A small block used to build a 3D image, like a pixel with depth.
glossary.Marching Cubes: A method that turns a grid of cube-like world pieces into a smooth surface.

glossary.LOC: Lines of code: a count of how many lines a program contains.
glossary.pull request: A proposal to add your code changes to a shared project, usually asking others to review them first.
glossary.AI agent: An autonomous computer program that can carry out tasks.
